subject: do
title: DO model sheet
description: Every model and algorithm in the 2026 final scope, one card each, checked against the course notes. Page numbers are the printed page numbers of the notes. Diagrams use made-up example data.
extraTitle: Also in past papers (not in final scope)

cards.title: Max-flow model and net flow
cards.summary: Send as much material as possible from the source $s$ to the sink $t$ of a directed network without exceeding any arc capacity. No costs.

variables.meaning: flow on arc $(i,j)$
capacity of arc $(i,j)$ (given)
amount sent from $s$ to $t$ (the flow value)

constraints.meaning: source: $F$ more leaves $s$ than enters it
conservation (node balance): what comes in goes out at every intermediate node
sink: $F$ more enters $t$ than leaves it
capacity: no arc carries more than its capacity

points: It is an LP; with integer capacities there is always an integer max flow.
Net flow: $f(i,j) = x_{ij} - x_{ji}$ (can be negative).
Skew-symmetry (antisymmetry): $f(i,j) = x_{ij} - x_{ji} = -(x_{ji} - x_{ij}) = -f(j,i)$.
Conservation in net flow: $\sum_l f(i,l) = 0$ for every $i \ne s,t$, and $f(s) = -f(t)$.
Value of a flow: $\text{val}(F) = \sum_{e \text{ out of } s} f(e) = \sum_{e \text{ into } t} f(e)$.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf p. 7 (§1.2, eqs. 6–10); net flow and skew-symmetry: NetworkFlowP.pdf pp. 3–4 (§2)

cards.title: Residual network and augmenting paths
cards.summary: The residual network $G_x$ shows where more flow can still be sent, given the current flow $x$. Each arc is replaced by a forward arc (spare capacity) and a reverse arc (flow that can be cancelled). An augmenting path is an $s \to t$ path in $G_x$.
points: Forward residual capacity: $r_{ij} = u_{ij} - x_{ij}$.
Reverse residual capacity: $r_{ji} = x_{ij}$ (sending back cancels flow).
$G_x$ keeps only the arcs with $r_{ij} > 0$.
Capacity of an augmenting path: $\delta(P) = \min\{r_{ij} : (i,j) \in P\}$.
Augmenting by $\delta(P)$: $r_{ij} \leftarrow r_{ij} - \delta(P)$ and $r_{ji} \leftarrow r_{ji} + \delta(P)$ on every arc of $P$.
No augmenting path left means the flow is maximum.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 14–15 (§1.6); NetworkFlowP.pdf pp. 7–8 (§4.1–4.2)

cards.title: s–t cut, cap(A, B) and max-flow = min-cut
cards.summary: An s–t cut $(A,B)$ splits the nodes into two disjoint sets with $s \in A$ and $t \in B$. Its capacity counts only the arcs that go from $A$ to $B$. Every flow is at most every cut, and the largest flow equals the smallest cut.
points: $\text{cap}(A,B) = \sum_{e \text{ out of } A} c_e$: arcs $A \to B$ only, never $B \to A$.
Cut-set: the arcs that begin in $A$ and end in $B$.
Flow value lemma: $\text{val}(F) = \sum_{e \text{ out of } A} f(e) - \sum_{e \text{ into } A} f(e)$ for any cut.
Weak duality: $\text{val}(F) \le \text{cap}(A,B)$ for every flow and every cut.
Max-flow min-cut theorem: $\max_F \text{val}(F) = \min_{(A,B)} \text{cap}(A,B)$.
If $\text{val}(F) = \text{cap}(A,B)$, then $F$ is a max flow and $(A,B)$ is a min cut.

images.alt: An s–t cut on the network s, a, b, t. A = {s, a} is shaded and B = {b, t}; a dashed line separates them. Arcs a→t (3), a→b (2) and s→b (3) go from A to B and are drawn in orange, so cap(A, B) = 3 + 2 + 3 = 8. Arc b→a (1) goes from B to A, is grey and is not counted.

cards.example: In the picture, $A = \{s, a\}$: the arcs $a \to t$, $a \to b$ and $s \to b$ cross from $A$ to $B$, so $\text{cap}(A,B) = 3 + 2 + 3 = 8$. The arc $b \to a$ goes backwards and is not counted.
cards.source: NetworkFlowP.pdf pp. 5–7 (§3, Definitions 1–4, Lemmas 1–2, Theorem 1); DisCopt.pdf pp. 16–17 (Definitions 1.5–1.6, Theorems 1.9 and 1.12)

cards.title: Ford–Fulkerson (max-flow min-cut) algorithm
cards.summary: Start with zero flow and keep pushing flow along augmenting paths in the residual network until none is left. The flow is then maximum, and the nodes still reachable from $s$ give a minimum cut.
steps: Start with $x = 0$, so $r_{ij} = u_{ij}$ on every arc.
Build the residual network $G_x$.
While $G_x$ has a directed path $P$ from $s$ to $t$: send $\delta(P) = \min_{(i,j) \in P} r_{ij}$ along it.
Update: $r_{ij} \leftarrow r_{ij} - \delta(P)$, $r_{ji} \leftarrow r_{ji} + \delta(P)$, and add $\delta(P)$ to the total flow.
Stop when there is no $s \to t$ path in $G_x$: the flow is maximum.
Min cut: $A$ = the nodes reachable from $s$ in the last $G_x$, $B$ = the rest. Then $\text{cap}(A,B)$ = max flow.
points: With integer (or rational) finite capacities it stops after finitely many steps.
Max flow = sum of all the $\delta(P)$ sent = flow out of $s$ = flow into $t$.

images.alt: Ford–Fulkerson on a four-node network in three panels. 1: capacities s→a 4, s→b 3, a→b 2, b→a 1, a→t 3, b→t 5. 2: a maximum flow of value 7, shown as flow/capacity: s→a 4/4, s→b 3/3, a→b 1/2, b→a 0/1, a→t 3/3, b→t 4/5. 3: the residual network with grey reverse arcs; no path from s to t is left, only s is reachable, so A = {s} and cap(A, B) = 4 + 3 = 7 = the max flow.

cards.example: Lecturer’s worked example: three augmenting paths carry $5 + 1 + 3 = 9$; afterwards only $c$ can be reached from $s$, so $A = \{s, c\}$, $B = \{b, d, e, t\}$ and $\text{cap}(A,B) = 9$ = max flow.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 13–17 (§1.6, the algorithm box on p. 16, Remark 1.11); NetworkFlowP.pdf p. 9 (§4.4); FordFulkerson.pdf pp. 1–3 (worked example, the cut from the reachable nodes on p. 3)

cards.title: The genetic algorithm loop
cards.summary: A GA keeps a population of $N$ chromosomes (candidate solutions, e.g. bit strings) and improves it generation by generation, copying nature: the fittest survive and breed.
steps: Create an initial population $G(0)$ of $N$ random chromosomes.
Evaluate the fitness of every chromosome and rank them.
Elitism: copy the best few (e.g. 10% of $N$) unchanged into $G(t+1)$.
Selection: pick pairs of parents, favouring fitter ones (tournament selection).
Crossover: each pair of parents makes two children (single- or double-point).
Mutation: flip each bit of each child with a small probability $p_\mu$.
The children fill the rest of $G(t+1)$; repeat from step 2 until the fitness values are close to each other (small standard deviation) or a maximum number of generations.
points: Balances exploiting good solutions (selection, elitism) and exploring the search space (crossover, mutation).
Needs no mathematical model, only a way to evaluate fitness. Constraints can be handled with a penalty (the lecturer’s knapsack code subtracts $R \cdot$ overweight).
Direct version for TSP / QAP: permutations, swap (path) crossover, no mutation.

images.alt: The GA loop as a row of boxes: Initial population, Fitness, Selection (tournament), Crossover, Mutation, New generation (+ elitism), with an arrow from New generation back to Fitness labelled "repeat until the stopping rule (e.g. max generations)".

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 52–55 (§3.4, the GA steps on p. 55); DiscreteGAcode.pdf pp. 1–2

cards.title: GA operators: elitism, tournament, crossover, mutation
cards.summary: The operators that turn generation $G(t)$ into $G(t+1)$. Elitism keeps the best, tournament selection picks good parents, crossover mixes two parents and mutation adds small random changes.
points: Elitism: the best (e.g. 10%) of $G(t)$ go straight into $G(t+1)$; the other 90% are made pairwise by selection, crossover and mutation.
Tournament selection: pick two different chromosomes at random and keep the fitter one as parent $A$; repeat for parent $B$ (a chromosome may be picked again).
Single-point crossover: one cut point; the two parents swap everything after it.
Double-point crossover (lecturer’s code): random positions $n_1 < n_2$; the parents swap the genes in positions $n_1, n_1 + 1, \dots, n_2$ (inclusive). Genes outside stay.
Mutation: for each bit, if random $< p_\mu$ flip it ($x_j \leftarrow 1 - x_j$). $p_\mu$ is small (the code uses $10^{-3}$) and keeps diversity.

images.alt: Double-point crossover and mutation on 5-bit strings. Parents x1 = 10101 and x2 = 01110 with cut lines around positions 3 and 4 (n1 = 3, n2 = 4); the segments 10 and 11 are swapped, giving children y1 = 10111 and y2 = 01100. Below, mutation flips one bit: 10111 becomes 10011.

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 52–54 (§3.4.1–3.4.2, Figs. 36–38); DiscreteGAcode.pdf p. 1 (tournament: two random indices, the fitter kept) and p. 2 (crossover loop “for l = n1 to n2”, mutation)

cards.title: Annealing, equilibrium distribution and the Metropolis rule
cards.summary: Physical annealing heats a solid and cools it slowly so its particles settle into a low-energy, ordered state. At a fixed temperature the system reaches thermal equilibrium, where state $x$ has the Boltzmann probability below. SA treats the objective as the energy and uses the Metropolis rule to sample this distribution.
points: Equilibrium (Boltzmann, stationary) distribution: $\pi_T(x) = \dfrac{e^{-E(x)/T}}{Z}$, with $Z = \sum_y e^{-E(y)/T}$.
As $T \to 0$, $\pi_T$ puts all its mass on the minimum-energy states, i.e. the optimum.
Metropolis acceptance (minimising): $A_{xy}(T) = \min\{1, e^{-(f(y) - f(x))/T}\}$. A better $y$ is always accepted; a worse one with probability $e^{-\Delta f/T}$, accepted if random$(0,1) <$ that.
Why Metropolis: $\pi_T$ can’t be sampled directly ($Z$ sums over every state). Metropolis builds a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is $\pi_T$, using only the difference $f(y) - f(x)$.
Accepting some worse moves lets SA escape local minima; high $T$ accepts many, low $T$ almost none.

images.alt: Two plots. Left: Metropolis acceptance probability P = min(1, e^(−ΔE/T)) against ΔE from 0 to 300 for T = 300, 100 and 30; it falls faster at lower T. The marked point ΔE = 100, T = 100 gives P = e^−1 = 0.368, and r = 0.25 < 0.368 means accept. Right: the Boltzmann distribution π(x) = e^(−E(x)/T)/Z over eight states with energies 5, 3, 6, 1, 4, 7, 2, 5; at T = 5 the bars are spread out, at T = 0.7 most of the mass is on x4, the minimum (E = 1).

cards.example: DOEXAM2021: $\Delta E = 100$, $T = 100$: $P = e^{-1} = 0.368$. With $r = 0.25 < 0.368$, accept the worse solution.
cards.source: Acceptance rule: DisCopt.pdf p. 50 (§3.3, eq. 101). Physical annealing, thermal equilibrium and “why Metropolis”: Assignment II 2026 Q1. The Boltzmann formula and the Markov-chain reason are the standard ones (as in the Assignment II solution), not written out in the notes.

cards.title: Simulated annealing algorithm
cards.summary: Two loops: the inner loop runs a Metropolis chain of $L_t$ trial moves at a fixed temperature $T_t$; the outer loop lowers the temperature. SA needs no mathematical model, only a way to make a trial solution $y$ from $x$ (e.g. swap two cities).
steps: Choose $T_0$, the chain length $L$, the stopping value $\varepsilon$ and a starting solution $x$; compute $f(x)$.
While $T > \varepsilon$, repeat $L$ times: generate a trial $y$ from $x$.
If $f(y) \le f(x)$ accept $y$; else accept it if $e^{-(f(y) - f(x))/T} >$ random$(0,1)$. If accepted, $x := y$.
After the $L$ trials, cool: $T_{t+1} = \alpha T_t$ (e.g. $\alpha = 0.9$), and repeat.
Stop when $T_t \le \varepsilon$; report the best solution found.
points: Cooling schedule: initial $T_0$ (acceptance ratio near 1), chain length $L_t$ (e.g. $10n$), decrement rule, stopping rule.
Simple decrement: $T_{t+1} = \alpha T_t$ with $\alpha \in (0.9, 0.97)$.
Slow cooling gives the chain time to reach equilibrium at each $T$.

images.alt: A step plot of the cooling schedule T(k+1) = α·T(k) with α = 0.85: the temperature starts at 100 and drops in steps towards 0 over 30 outer iterations. The title notes that at each T an inner loop of Metropolis moves runs until equilibrium.

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 50–51 (§3.3 SA algorithm, §3.3.1 cooling schedule, Remark 3.4); sa.pdf p. 1 (the lecturer’s pseudocode, T = 0.9T)

cards.title: Relaxed problem and bounds
cards.summary: The relaxation of an integer (or binary) program drops the integrality: $x_j \in \{0,1\}$ becomes $0 \le x_j \le 1$ (or integer becomes real). The relaxed problem is easier (an LP for a linear model) and its optimum bounds the integer optimum.
points: Minimisation: relaxed optimum = lower bound; any feasible integer solution = upper bound.
Maximisation: relaxed optimum = upper bound; any feasible integer solution = lower bound.
Relaxed solution infeasible → the integer problem is infeasible.
Relaxed solution already integer → it is optimal for the integer problem.
Quadratic problems (QAP, QKP, bisection) are relaxed the same way and solved with a suitable solver.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 45–47 (§3.2 and §3.2.2 LP-based B&B); vertex cover relaxation p. 36

cards.title: Branch and bound
cards.summary: “Intelligent enumeration”: solve the relaxation, branch on a fractional variable to make two subproblems, and delete subproblems that can’t contain a better solution. Shown here for minimisation (swap the bounds for maximisation).
steps: Find an initial feasible integer solution (e.g. by a heuristic): incumbent $x^*$ with upper bound $u(S)$.
Pick a subproblem $P(S_j)$ from the list (depth-first: the newest) and solve its relaxation: lower bound $l(S_j)$.
Delete it if (1) the relaxation is infeasible, (2) its solution is integer (update the incumbent if better), or (3) $l(S_j) > u(S)$: it can’t beat the incumbent.
Otherwise branch on the most fractional variable $\hat{x}_i$: $x_i \le \lfloor \hat{x}_i \rfloor$ and $x_i \ge \lceil \hat{x}_i \rceil$ (for 0-1: $x_i = 0$ and $x_i = 1$), and add both to the list.
Stop when the list is empty; the incumbent is optimal.
points: Bounding = deletion cases (2) and (3); infeasible subproblems are deleted too.
Speed depends on a good initial incumbent and tight relaxation bounds.

images.alt: Two separate examples. Left: the LP feasible region of a small two-variable maximisation, with orange dots for the integer points inside, a blue star for the fractional LP optimum (the bound) and a red square for the best integer point. Right: a branch and bound tree for a maximisation: the root (LP 10.5, x1 = 2.5) branches into x1 ≤ 2 (LP 9.8, x2 = 1.4) and x1 ≥ 3 (infeasible, deleted, case 1); x1 ≤ 2 branches into x2 ≤ 1 (LP 9, integer, becomes the incumbent, case 2) and x2 ≥ 2 (LP 8.6 ≤ 9, deleted by bound, case 3).

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 45–49 (§3.2, deletion cases (a)–(b) and infeasibility on pp. 45–46, steps in §3.2.3 pp. 48–49)

cards.title: Linear assignment problem (LAP)
cards.summary: Assign $n$ applicants to $n$ jobs, one each, at minimum total cost $c_{ij}$. Also called weighted bipartite (perfect) matching.

variables.meaning: 1 if applicant $i$ is assigned to job $j$
cost of applicant $i$ doing job $j$ (given)

constraints.meaning: every applicant gets exactly one job
every job gets exactly one applicant
binary

points: Linear: the cost of a pair doesn’t depend on the other pairs.
The LP relaxation already has an integer optimum, so LAP is easy (polynomial).
Perfect matching form: $\max \sum_e c_e x_e$ s.t. $\sum_{e \text{ at } i} x_e = 1$ for each vertex.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 9–11 (§1.4, eqs. 14–17; matching form eqs. 18–20)

cards.title: LAP as a minimum-cost flow
cards.summary: LAP (and the transportation problem) is a min-cost flow network with no intermediate nodes: one supply node per worker, one demand node per job, and an arc from each worker to each job with cost $c_{ij}$.
points: Min-cost flow: $\min \sum c_{ij} x_{ij}$ s.t. $\sum_j x_{ij} - \sum_j x_{ji} = b_i$ for each $i$, $0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij}$.
LAP: $b_i = 1$ at each worker (supply), $b_j = -1$ at each job (demand).
The picture adds a source $s$ and a sink $t$ with capacity-1 arcs and sends $n$ units: the same thing.
Integer data give an integer optimal flow, so the flow is a valid assignment.

images.alt: LAP as a minimum-cost flow network: a source s with capacity-1 arcs to workers W1, W2, W3, orange arcs from every worker to every job J1, J2, J3 with cost c_ij and capacity 1, and capacity-1 arcs from each job to the sink t. The caption says to send n = 3 units from s to t at minimum cost.

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 8–9 (§1.3, eqs. 11–13, Remarks 1.2 and 1.4)

cards.title: Quadratic assignment problem (QAP)
cards.summary: Place $n$ facilities at $n$ locations, one each. The cost depends on the flow between every pair of facilities times the distance between the locations they get, so it depends on pairs of assignments.

variables.meaning: 1 if facility $i$ is placed at location $j$
flow between facilities $i$ and $j$ (given)
distance between locations $k$ and $l$ (given)
cost of placing facility $i$ at location $j$ (given)

model.objective: \min \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{l=1}^n f_{ij}\, d_{kl}\, x_{ik}\, x_{jl} + \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}\, x_{ij}

constraints.meaning: every location gets exactly one facility
every facility goes to exactly one location
binary (so $X$ is a permutation matrix)

points: Quadratic: the term $x_{ik} x_{jl}$ is a product, “facility $i$ at $k$ and facility $j$ at $l$”, costing $f_{ij} d_{kl}$.
Permutation form (Koopmans–Beckmann): $\min_{\pi \in S_n} \sum_i \sum_j f_{ij} d_{\pi(i)\pi(j)} + \sum_i b_{i\pi(i)}$.
There are $n!$ feasible assignments; QAP is one of the hardest problems (no exact method for $n > 20$ in reasonable time).
LAP vs QAP: same assignment constraints, but LAP’s cost is linear (each pair on its own) and easy; QAP’s cost couples pairs of assignments and is NP-hard.

images.alt: LAP next to QAP. Left (LAP): workers W1–W3 joined to jobs J1–J3 by grey edges, with one feasible assignment in orange (W1–J2, W2–J1, W3–J3); x_ij = 1 if worker i does job j, every worker one job and every job one worker. Right (QAP): facilities A, B, C with flows f_AB = 5 and f_BC = 1, dashed arrows placing them at locations L1, L2, L3 whose distances are d = 3, 4, 2. Placing A at L1 and B at L2 costs f_AB · d_12 = 5 · 3, which depends on pairs of assignments (x_ij · x_kl), so the cost is quadratic; there are n! assignments.

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 32–34 (§2.8, eq. 69; §2.8.1 quadratic integer programming formulation, eqs. 71–75)

cards.title: Clique, maximal and maximum clique
cards.summary: A clique is a set of vertices that are all joined to each other. A maximal clique can’t be extended by another vertex; a maximum clique is a largest one (its size is the clique number $\omega(G)$). Every maximum clique is maximal, not the other way round.

variables.meaning: 1 if vertex $i$ is in the clique

constraints.meaning: two vertices that are not adjacent can’t both be chosen
binary

points: A clique in $G$ is an independent set in the complement $\bar{G}$ (edges exactly where $G$ has none).
So max clique of $G$ = maximum independent set of $\bar{G}$.
Maximum clique is NP-hard.

images.alt: Left: a graph G on vertices 1–6 with edges 12, 13, 14, 23, 24, 34, 45, 46, 56. {1, 2, 3, 4} is shaded with its six edges in orange: the maximum clique (ω = 4). {4, 5, 6} with blue edges is a maximal clique but not maximum. Right: the complement Ḡ, with edges exactly where G has none (15, 16, 25, 26, 35, 36); {1, 2, 3, 4} has no edges there, so it is a maximum independent set of Ḡ.

cards.source: Standard formulation, not in the notes (no course notes on cliques were found; the scope and E-Science Exam 2021 Q2(d) name the problem)

cards.title: Planted clique
cards.summary: A random graph with a clique of known size $k$ hidden in it, used to test clique-finding methods: we know a $k$-clique is there and must find it among random edges.
steps: Start with $n$ vertices $V = \{1, \dots, n\}$ and no edges.
Choose $k < n$ vertices at random.
Join every pair of the chosen vertices: they form a $k$-clique.
Add every other edge independently with probability $p$ (a random graph $G(n, p)$).
points: The planted clique is a clique of size $k$, so $\omega(G) \ge k$.
For small $p$ and large enough $k$ it is the maximum clique; finding it is hard when $k$ is small.

images.alt: A planted clique with n = 14, k = 5 and p = 0.18: fourteen vertices on a circle; vertices 1, 4, 7, 10 and 12 are shaded and all ten edges among them are orange (the guaranteed 5-clique); the other edges, added at random with probability p, are grey. The caption lists the steps: start with V = {1, …, n}, choose k vertices, join every pair of them, add every other edge independently with probability p.

cards.source: Standard construction, not in the notes (E-Science Exam 2021 Q2(d) asks for “one way of creating a planted clique of size k”)

cards.title: Maximum independent set (MIS)
cards.summary: An independent set is a set of vertices with no edge between any two of them. The maximum independent set problem asks for a largest one. It is the clique problem on the complement graph.

variables.meaning: 1 if vertex $i$ is in the set

constraints.meaning: the two ends of an edge can’t both be chosen
binary

points: Clique vs MIS: the same model, but the constraint is over non-edges (clique) or edges (MIS).
$S$ is independent in $G$ ⇔ $S$ is a clique in $\bar{G}$.
$S$ is independent ⇔ $V \setminus S$ is a vertex cover, so max independent set = $n$ − min vertex cover.
cards.source: Standard formulation, not in the notes (vertex cover itself: DisCopt.pdf pp. 34–35, §2.9)

cards.title: Graph bisection (max-bisection)
cards.summary: Split the $n$ vertices (n even) of a weighted undirected graph into two halves of equal size, $V_1$ and $V_2$, so that the total weight of the edges between the halves is as large as possible. The notes use the max version.

variables.meaning: $x_i = 1$ if $i \in V_1$, $x_i = -1$ if $i \in V_2$
weight of edge $(i,j)$ (0 if there is no edge)

constraints.meaning: as many $+1$s as $-1$s: the halves are the same size
every vertex is on one side

points: $1 - x_i x_j = 2$ if $i$ and $j$ are on different sides, 0 if on the same side.
Why ¼: the double sum counts each edge twice ($w_{ij}$ and $w_{ji}$), and each crossing edge gives 2, so $2 \times 2 = 4$; ¼ leaves exactly the crossing weight.
Symmetry: if $x$ is feasible so is $-x$ (swap the halves), with the same objective.
It is an integer quadratic program (the $x_i x_j$ term).

images.alt: Max-bisection of six vertices: V1 = {1, 2, 3} with x_i = +1 on the left, V2 = {4, 5, 6} with x_i = −1 on the right. The crossing edges in red are 1–4 (4), 2–4 (5), 2–5 (1) and 3–6 (2); the edges inside a half (1–2, 2–3, 4–5, 5–6) are grey. Σ x_i = 0, crossing edges give 1 − x_i x_j = 2, and ¼ ΣΣ w_ij (1 − x_i x_j) = 4 + 5 + 1 + 2 = 12.

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 39–40 (§2.11)

cards.title: Max-cut (and how it differs from bisection)
cards.summary: Split the vertices into two sets $S$ and $V \setminus S$ of any sizes so that the weight of the edges between them is as large as possible. Same as max-bisection without the equal-size constraint.

variables.meaning: $x_i = 1$ if $i \in S$, $-1$ otherwise

model.objective: \max\ f(x) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} w_{ij}\,(1 - x_i x_j)

constraints.meaning: the only constraint: no balance constraint

points: ½ instead of ¼: the sum runs over $i < j$, so each edge is counted once.
Bisection = max-cut + $\sum_i x_i = 0$.
Max-cut is NP-complete, but min cut (s–t) is polynomial with Ford–Fulkerson.
Max-$k$-cut splits $V$ into $k$ parts; max-cut is $k = 2$.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 40–41 (§2.12, eqs. 97–98)

cards.title: Facility location (fixed charge, capacitated, single source)
cards.summary: Choose which of $m$ potential facilities (depots) to open and which open facility serves each of $n$ customers, minimising opening costs plus serving costs.

variables.meaning: 1 if a facility is opened at potential location $i$
1 if customer $j$ is served from the facility at $i$
fixed cost of opening $i$; cost of serving $j$ from $i$ (given)
demand of customer $j$; capacity of facility $i$ (given)

constraints.meaning: every customer is served by exactly one facility (single source)
only an open facility can serve a customer
capacity: the demand served by $i$ is at most its capacity (drop this for the uncapacitated problem)
binary

points: First term: distribution cost; second: fixed opening cost. The number of depots is a trade-off between the two.
Uncapacitated (UFLP): no capacity constraint; each customer goes to its cheapest open facility.
p-median: no fixed costs, $\sum_i y_i = p$.

images.alt: Facility location: four candidate facilities drawn as squares; F1 and F4 are open (filled, y = 1) and F2 and F3 are closed (empty, y = 0). Nine customers (blue dots) are each joined by a dashed line to the one open facility that serves them. The caption repeats: each customer is served by exactly one facility, Σ_i x_ij = 1; only open facilities serve, x_ij ≤ y_i; cost = Σ f_i y_i (opening) + Σ c_ij x_ij (serving).

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 27–30 (§2.5, eqs. 51–57; p-median eqs. 58–63)

cards.title: Asymmetric TSP model (subtour elimination)
cards.summary: Visit each of $n$ cities exactly once and return home at minimum cost, where $c_{ij}$ may differ from $c_{ji}$ (a directed graph).

variables.meaning: 1 if the salesman goes directly from city $i$ to city $j$
cost of travelling from $i$ to $j$ (given)

constraints.meaning: every city is entered exactly once
every city is left exactly once

constraints.math: \sum_{i \in S} \sum_{j \in S} x_{ij} \le |S| - 1 \quad S \subset V,\ 2 \le |S| \le n - 2
constraints.meaning: subtour elimination: the cities of $S$ can’t form a closed loop on their own
binary

points: Without subtour elimination, a solution can be several separate cycles (subtours) that still satisfy the in/out constraints.
There are exponentially many subtour constraints; in practice add only the violated ones and re-solve.

images.alt: Left: seven cities where every city has one arc in and one arc out, but the arcs form two subtours, 1→2→1 (red) and 3→4→5→6→7→3 (blue); for S = {1, 2}, x12 + x21 = 2 > |S| − 1 = 1, so the subtour constraint is violated. Right: a valid tour, one Hamiltonian cycle 1→2→3→4→5→6→7→1, with the subtour elimination constraint Σ_{i,j∈S} x_ij ≤ |S| − 1, 2 ≤ |S| ≤ n−2 (DisCopt eq. 37), and for the STSP 3 ≤ |S| ≤ n−3 (eq. 41).

cards.example: 7 cities: 1→2→1 and 3→4→5→6→7→3 meet both assignment constraints but are two subtours. $S = \{1, 2\}$: $x_{12} + x_{21} = 2 > |S| - 1 = 1$.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 20–21 (§2.2.1, eqs. 33–38)

cards.title: Symmetric TSP model
cards.summary: The TSP on an undirected complete graph, $c_{ij} = c_{ji}$: the direction of travel doesn’t matter, so there is one variable per edge and every city has degree 2 in the tour.

variables.meaning: 1 if edge $e$ is in the tour
cost (length) of edge $e$ (given)

constraints.meaning: every city has two tour edges (in and out), i.e. is visited exactly once
subtour elimination: the edges inside $S$ can’t close a cycle
binary

points: $\delta(i)$: the edges at vertex $i$; $E(S)$: the edges with both ends in $S$.
$|S| \ge 3$ because an undirected subtour needs at least 3 cities (a 2-city loop would use one edge twice).
Equivalent form with $x_{ij}$, $i < j$: $\sum_{i<k} x_{ik} + \sum_{j>k} x_{kj} = 2$ for every $k$.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 21–22 (§2.2.2, eqs. 39–46)

cards.title: TSP: tours, route counts, Hamiltonian vs Eulerian
cards.summary: A tour is a Hamiltonian cycle: it visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start. An Eulerian cycle instead uses every edge exactly once (vertices may repeat). TSP is NP-hard because the number of tours grows like $n!$.
points: Asymmetric TSP, home city fixed: $(n-1)!$ tours ($n!$ if any city can be home).
Symmetric TSP, home city fixed: $\frac{1}{2}(n-1)!$ (each tour and its reverse are the same).
Hamiltonian: every vertex once. Eulerian: every edge once; exists in a connected graph iff every degree is even.
Triangle inequality: $c_{ij} + c_{jk} \ge c_{ik}$ (e.g. Euclidean distances); Christofides needs it.

images.alt: Two graphs on vertices 1–5. Left: a Hamiltonian cycle 1-2-5-3-4-1 in orange visits every vertex once; the edges 1–5 and 2–3 stay unused (grey). Right: an Eulerian cycle 1-2-5-3-4-5-1 in blue uses every edge once; vertex 5 is visited twice and every degree is even.

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 19–20 (§2.2, route counts and Remark 2.1); Eulerian walk: p. 24 (§2.3.2, step 5)

cards.title: Minimum spanning tree (MST)
cards.summary: A spanning tree connects all $n$ vertices of an undirected graph with no cycles, using exactly $n - 1$ edges. The MST is the one of least total cost. It is step 1 of Christofides.

variables.meaning: 1 if edge $e$ is in the tree

constraints.meaning: connected: at least one tree edge leaves every set $S$ ($\delta(S)$ = edges with one end in $S$)
a tree on $n$ vertices has $n - 1$ edges
binary

points: Deleting one edge of an optimal tour gives a spanning tree, so cost(MST) ≤ OPT (used in the 3/2 bound).

images.alt: A minimum spanning tree on six points A–F: the five orange tree edges are A–F, B–F, E–F, D–F and C–D; the other edges of the complete graph are faint grey. Title: connects all, no cycles, n−1 = 5 edges, minimum weight.

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 11–13 (§1.5, eqs. 21–25)

cards.title: 2-opt heuristic (“two optimal heuristics”)
cards.summary: A local search for the TSP: repeatedly remove two non-adjacent edges of the tour and reconnect the two paths the other way (reversing the segment between them) whenever that shortens the tour. It ends in a 2-optimal tour, a local (not necessarily global) optimum. The scope’s “two optimal heuristics for TSP” is read here as 2-opt; that is an inference.
steps: Start with a tour $T = (c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n, c_1)$ of length $D$.
For $i = 1, 2, \dots$ and $j = i + 2, \dots$: break the links $(c_i, c_{i+1})$ and $(c_j, c_{j+1})$.
Reconnect with $(c_i, c_j)$ and $(c_{i+1}, c_{j+1})$: $\hat{T} = (c_1, \dots, c_i, c_j, \dots, c_{i+1}, c_{j+1}, \dots, c_1)$ (the segment is reversed).
If $\text{dist}(i,i+1) + \text{dist}(j,j+1) > \text{dist}(i,j) + \text{dist}(i+1,j+1)$, the new tour is shorter: $T := \hat{T}$, update $D$ and start again.
When no 2-opt move improves $T$, stop: $T$ is 2-optimal.
points: Two tours are 2-adjacent if one is obtained from the other by deleting two edges and adding two edges; $N(T)$ is the set of them.
Only the four changed edges need comparing, not the whole tour.
3-opt: the same with three edges (3-adjacent, 3-optimal).

images.alt: A 2-opt move on seven cities. Before: tour 1-2-5-4-3-6-7-1 of length 11.26, with the crossing edges (2,5) and (3,6) in red. After: those two edges are removed, the segment 5-4-3 is reversed to 3-4-5 and the edges (2,3) and (5,6) are added in green, giving tour 1-2-3-4-5-6-7-1 of length 8.42. Δ = d23 + d56 − d25 − d36 < 0, so the move is accepted; repeat until no 2-opt move improves (2-optimal).

cards.example: Notes: $T = (c_1, \dots, c_7, c_1)$, $i = 1$, $j = 3$ gives $(c_1, c_3, c_2, c_4, c_5, c_6, c_7, c_1)$. With $c_1$ fixed the notes list 10 such neighbours.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 25–26 (§2.3.3, Fig. 28, eqs. 49–50, the basic and detailed steps)

cards.title: α-approximation algorithm
cards.summary: An algorithm $A$ for a minimisation problem is an $\alpha$-approximation ($\alpha \ge 1$) if, for every instance $I$, it finds a feasible solution in polynomial time with cost at most $\alpha$ times the optimum. Unlike a heuristic, the guarantee holds on every instance.
points: Minimisation: $A(I) \le \alpha \, OPT(I)$ for all $I$.
Maximisation: $A(I) \ge \frac{1}{\alpha} OPT(I)$ for all $I$.
Three requirements: polynomial time, always feasible, the bound on every instance.
A heuristic (e.g. 2-opt) has no such guarantee.
Examples: Christofides for metric STSP ($\alpha = 3/2$); LP rounding for vertex cover ($\alpha = 2$).

images.alt: A number line with OPT on the left, ALG in the middle and α·OPT (α = 3/2) on the right; the shaded band from OPT to α·OPT is where the algorithm’s cost must lie. Caption: minimisation, OPT ≤ cost(ALG) ≤ α·OPT for every instance, in polynomial time (α ≥ 1).

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 22–23 (§2.3 and §2.3.1, eqs. 47–48)

cards.title: Christofides algorithm for the STSP
cards.summary: An approximation algorithm for the symmetric TSP whose tour is at most 3/2 times the optimal length (when the distances satisfy the triangle inequality). It uses the fact that every graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices.
steps: Find a minimum spanning tree $T$ of the graph.
Find the vertices with odd degree in $T$ (always an even number of them).
Find a minimum-weight perfect matching $M$ of those odd vertices (pair them up with the shortest edges).
Add the matching edges to $T$ (an edge in both is doubled): now every degree is even.
Construct an Eulerian circuit of $T \cup M$ (every edge exactly once).
Delete repeated vertices (shortcut): the remaining order is a Hamiltonian cycle, the TSP tour.
points: Why 3/2: cost($T$) ≤ OPT (drop an edge of the optimal tour), cost($M$) ≤ OPT/2, and shortcutting never adds length (triangle inequality). So tour ≤ 3/2 · OPT.
The notes state the 3/2 guarantee; the reason above is the standard proof, not in the notes.

images.alt: Christofides on six points A–F in five panels. 1: the MST T (edges A–F, B–F, E–F, D–F, C–D). 2: the odd-degree vertices O = {A, B, C, E} are filled; |O| = 4, always even. 3: the minimum perfect matching M on O, dashed blue edges A–E and B–C. 4: T ∪ M has all degrees even, giving the Euler circuit A-E-F-D-C-B-F-A. 5: shortcutting the repeated F gives the tour A-E-F-D-C-B-A of length 10.35 (the optimum is 10.05). Caption: why ≤ 3/2·OPT for metric STSP: cost(T) ≤ OPT, cost(M) ≤ OPT/2, and shortcutting never increases the cost (triangle inequality).

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 23–24 (§2.3.2, Fig. 27, steps 1–6); the 3/2 proof is standard, not in the notes

cards.title: Vertex cover (unweighted and weighted)
cards.summary: A vertex cover of an undirected graph is a set of vertices that touches every edge: for each edge $(i,j)$, $i$ or $j$ (or both) is in the cover. Find one of minimum size, or of minimum total weight $c_i$.

variables.meaning: 1 if vertex $i$ is in the cover
weight of vertex $i$ (weighted version; all 1 for the unweighted one)

constraints.meaning: every edge has at least one end in the cover
binary

points: The unweighted version is also called cardinality vertex cover.
Special case of set cover: the elements are the edges, and each vertex is the set of edges it touches.
$C$ is a vertex cover ⇔ $V \setminus C$ is an independent set.
Decision version ($k$-vertex cover): is there a cover with at most $k$ vertices? Greedy kernel rule: a vertex of degree $\ge k + 1$ must be in the cover.
Application: place as few ATMs as possible so that every street has one.

images.alt: A graph on six vertices with edges 1–2, 1–3, 2–3, 2–4, 3–5, 4–5, 4–6 and 5–6. The minimum vertex cover C = {1, 2, 4, 5} is filled: every edge has at least one filled end (x_i + x_j ≥ 1). The unfilled vertices V \ C = {3, 6} have no edge between them, so they form an independent set.

cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 34–36 (§2.9, eqs. 85–90)

cards.title: Vertex cover: LP relaxation and ½-rounding (2-approximation)
cards.summary: Solve the LP relaxation of the weighted vertex cover model and put every vertex with value at least ½ into the cover. The result is always a cover and costs at most twice the optimum.
steps: Relax $x_i \in \{0,1\}$ to $x_i \ge 0$ and solve the LP: solution $\hat{x}$.
Round: $C = \{i \in V : \hat{x}_i \ge \frac{1}{2}\}$.
$C$ is a cover: for each edge $\hat{x}_i + \hat{x}_j \ge 1$, so $\max\{\hat{x}_i, \hat{x}_j\} \ge \frac{1}{2}$ and at least one end is taken.
Cost: $c^T \bar{x} = \sum_{\hat{x}_i \ge 1/2} c_i \le \sum_{\hat{x}_i \ge 1/2} 2 \hat{x}_i c_i \le 2 c^T \hat{x} \le 2 c^T x^*$.
points: $c^T \hat{x} \le c^T x^*$ because the relaxation is a lower bound (minimisation).
So the rounding is a 2-approximation for minimum-weight vertex cover.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 35–36 (§2.9, the rounding argument after eq. 90)

cards.title: Set covering
cards.summary: Choose a cheapest family of subsets $S_j$ (cost $c_j$) whose union covers every element (duty) $i$ of $S = \{1, \dots, m\}$.

variables.meaning: 1 if subset (work pattern) $S_j$ is chosen
1 if element $i$ is in $S_j$ (given)

constraints.meaning: every element is covered at least once
binary

points: Examples: air crew scheduling, doctors on call covering every procedure.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 29–32 (§2.6, eqs. 64–68)

cards.title: Knapsack and quadratic knapsack
cards.summary: Choose items of weight $w_i$ and value $v_i$ to maximise the total value without exceeding the weight limit $W$.

variables.meaning: 1 if item $i$ is put in the knapsack

constraints.meaning: the total weight is within the limit
binary

points: Quadratic knapsack: $\max \sum_j c_j x_j + \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \sum_{j=k+1}^n d_{kj} x_k x_j$ s.t. $\sum_j a_{ij} x_j \le b_i$, $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ (pairs of items add value).
Both are NP-hard; capital budgeting has the same form with several budget constraints.
cards.source: DisCopt.pdf pp. 18–19 (§2.1, eqs. 26–32 and the quadratic knapsack)
